#10404. 23 ways to handle tasks that trigger dread

Everyone has them: Tasks they dread. They can range from mundane or routine items that clog the calendar to difficult conversations and meetings that cause stress. Avoiding them doesn’t make them go away. It just makes the dread heavier. Figuring out how to get through them frees up the time and headspace they take up. 

We asked members of the Fast Company Impact Council how they handle tasks they dread. Here, 23 of them provide their best tips for getting them off your to-do list.

1. BODY-DOUBLE THE TASK

I don’t tackle them alone. We call it body doubling: pulling in a teammate for a focused session to knock out the task neither of us wants to face solo. It depends on the task at hand too! My default is our incredible chief of staff. She’s the left brain to my right brain. From there it’s our executive team if the task requires finance, operations, technology, etc. Consistently routing the task with the right team members keeps the business moving forward. — Cody Barbo, Trust & Will

2. JUST DO IT AND DO IT NOW

Dread is what you feel when you aren’t just doing it. Just do it. And when you do, more often than not you enter flow state, and you just keep doing stuff. — Eric Simons, Bolt.new

3. APPROACH IT LIKE AN ATHLETE

When I face a task I’d rather avoid, I try to tackle it right away, before I give myself a hundred reasons to postpone it. I approach these situations like an athlete: Discomfort is part of progress, not a reason to stop. Whether it’s a challenging negotiation or a difficult decision, I’ve learned to take action even when I don’t feel ready. Years of daily training and building at my company have taught me that motivation comes and goes, and discipline is the key to keeping you moving forward. You can’t always control how you feel about a task, but you can train yourself to show up and get it done anyway. — Victoria Repa, BetterMe

4. TAKE ONE SMALL STEP

In my mind, most dread comes from a task that has no clear definition or parameter. I’ve found it helpful to jump on the first physical step, small enough to finish in a few minutes (e.g., open the file, draft the subject line, pull last month’s numbers) and physically stop there to build next steps. This creates a sense of internal accountability. Once the task has a shape, the rest usually goes faster than the dread predicted. Also, if it still sits there after a week, that’s useful information: It may belong to someone else, or it may not need doing at all. — James Chester, WVN

5. CHIP AWAY EACH DAY

Momentum beats motivation. I start small and chip away a little each day. Procrastinating doesn’t buy you time, it just weighs you down, and eventually it crowds out the work you love. — Tami Rosen, executive board and advisor to technology and finance companies

6. TACKLE THEM FIRST, EARLY IN THE DAY

I do them first, and I make them smaller. Dread grows in the gap between knowing a task needs doing and starting it. So I close that gap early in the day, before anything else competes for my attention. If it’s big, I commit only to the first part. Momentum handles the rest. I’ve also learned to ask what the dread is telling me. Sometimes it’s a sign the task needs a conversation, not more effort, and the fastest way through is a call to the right person. — Megan Noel, Covista

7. NAME WHAT YOU DREAD AND WHY

Usually, people dread something because it is uncomfortable, ambiguous, or carries some sort of emotional weight. I try to name what I dread and why, instead of pretending the task itself is the problem. If it matters, do it and do it now, because avoidance compounds just like progress does. The things we put off usually get heavier, not lighter. — Ethan Braden, Texas A&M University

8. TAKE OUT THE TRASH DAY

A colleague once inspired me with her “take out the trash day,” dedicating a chunk of time each week to knock through dreaded tasks. With all the noise on Slack, texts, and email, I block an hour at the end of the week, mute my notifications, and cruise through. It’s how I take care of budgets, expenses, and the general paperwork, so I can get back to the creative work where I’m in my flow. Sometimes there’s a snack reward waiting at the end. — Courtney Brigham, Typeface

9. SET A REWARD FOR YOURSELF

I break it down into chunks, set a target date and time to complete each chunk, and then block out time and get it done. I also set a reward for myself after doing it. For example, I’ll get to have this great lunch after I finish it. It sounds silly, but it’s nice to have rewards after doing a project that is not enjoyable! — Felicia Curcuru, Binti

10. RELY ON PREPARATION

During dreaded high-stakes situations like meetings with multiple stakeholders or delivering sensitive performance-based feedback, I rely on preparation. Coming armed with a brief outline of mission-critical points ensures you stay on track and helps you recover if the conversation gets derailed. If I’m ruminating on a complex problem that I just can’t seem to crack, I put everything down and do something completely unrelated. Taking a walk, listening to a podcast, or even washing the dishes allows my brain to marinate, discover hidden connections, and eventually the solution becomes clear. — Celia Jones, FINN Partners

11. PRIORITIZE ACCORDINGLY

Tasks I dread are rarely the most important for our business, so I prioritize them accordingly. However, they tend to bubble up to the higher end of the list of less critical tasks. The longer they remain on my to-do list, the more days they get to impact my morale, so I’m motivated to get them done. — Brad Weber, InspiringApps

12. CONNECT IT TO OUTCOME

I try to stay positive by focusing on the value the task will create once it’s completed. I put it in the broader context of the goal it supports and the impact it will have. As a big-picture person, details can be challenging, but connecting the work to a meaningful outcome helps me stay motivated and push through with a positive mindset. — Chris K Bailey, Bailey Brand Consulting

13. TAKE THE MEDICINE ALL AT ONCE

I put them off. Then I bundle them up and take care of them all at once. Like medicine. It tastes bad but works. Sort of like Buckley’s cough and cold medicine. — Phillip Haid, Public Inc.

14. STOP AND MAP IT OUT

If I catch myself spending real time on something where I’m just going through the motions, I stop and map it out. What are the inputs, what am I doing with them, and what does the output need to look like? Once the process is clearly mapped, it’s usually pretty obvious that a lot of it doesn’t need me. Then I build an automation around it. I still get the result; I just skip the mundane part. — Mike Sewell, Gresham Smith

15. ASK WHETHER YOU’RE THE RIGHT PERSON TO DO IT

I try not to spend too much time negotiating with myself. If something needs to be done, I focus on the next step and start. Usually, the anticipation is worse than the task itself. As a CEO, I’ve also learned to ask whether I’m the right person to do it. There are many things I can do, but I don’t need to do all of them. Sometimes leadership means taking something on yourself. Other times it means trusting someone else to own it. What I try to avoid is letting something I don’t enjoy become something the organization has to wait for. — Yuping Huang, Quantum Computing Inc.

16. CARVE UP YOUR DAY

Technology marketing is constant context switching and rapid decision-making. If you’re not careful, a whole day passes without a minute of real thought or creativity. You give in to the “critical” transactions, and eventually the work that’s most critical to your job disappears entirely. So I carve up my day. Mornings are for content, strategy, and creative problem-solving. Midday is the transactional work. The last couple of hours go to administration and anything that wasn’t urgent. And if something that needs real creativity slips through until late in the day, it gets the first look the next morning, with fresh eyes. — Colby Proffitt, Seekr

17. DIVIDE IT INTO MANAGEABLE STEPS

When I face a task I dread, I focus on understanding what makes it difficult and what depends on completing it. This matters because postponing an uncomfortable responsibility does not remove it. It can affect decisions, relationships, and other people’s work. I divide the task into manageable steps, establish a clear deadline, and begin with the first action. For me, discipline is not about enjoying every responsibility. It is about addressing what needs to be done before hesitation becomes a larger problem. — Manuel Freire-Garabal, Gioya HEI

18. DO THE WORST THING FIRST

Do it first. I was told once that you should always do the worst thing on your to-do list first because the day then only gets better. Have stuck to it ever since. And never overlook the power of reward: For every annoying task give yourself a little treat in return. The promise of a future good thing coming your way works every time. — Helen Andrews, Johannes Leonardo

19. AUTOMATE THE MUNDANE

Recently, I’ve unlocked a new cheat code in chipping away at those dreaded tasks. When walking to work, I’ll start talking with my favorite large language model of the moment and we can hammer out 10 open items from unanswered Slack messages and emails to meeting recaps and other nagging tasks that can quickly pile up. When all the right connectors are in place, the efficiency unlock is tremendous and has been a game changer for knocking out those dreaded to-dos. — Matt Conlin, Fluent

20. KNOW WHEN THE TASK BELONGS TO SOMEONE ELSE

I like to understand every aspect of my business, even the things that don’t come naturally to me. I’m always open to learning something new, but I also recognize when something falls outside my skill set. I believe in knowing your strengths and surrounding yourself with people who bring expertise you don’t have. If it’s something I can tackle, I get it done. If someone else can do it better, I delegate. My time is best spent where I can make the greatest impact. — Kim Wileman, No Makeup Makeup

21. USE THE HEADWIND AS A TAILWIND

I once heard Jimmy Iovine, co-founder of Beats, talk about using a headwind as a tailwind, and it’s stuck with me ever since. If there’s something you hate doing, run towards it, not away from it. Delay is a false economy because it just extends the dread. Then I break it into tiny actions and get the first one done. Momentum beats motivation every time, and most tasks are never as bad as the story you’ve told yourself about them. — Emily Kortlang, Meaco

22. MEET IT AT YOUR COGNITIVE PEAK

I use power hours. I know my brain is sharpest late in the evening or early in the morning, so I save the tasks I would normally procrastinate on for that window. I don’t do it every day. The idea is simple: Dreaded work takes far less energy when you meet it at your cognitive peak, so an hour or two of focus can clear what would otherwise linger for weeks. — Muneer Panjwani, Engage for Good | The Halo Awards

23. ATTACK THE FIRST FIVE MINUTES

I try to attack the first five minutes rather than the whole task. Dread grows in the space between knowing you have to do something and starting it. Once I take action, the task usually gets a lot less intimidating. — Ran Mullins, Psympl

#10403. Nintendo Switch 2 emulation on Android already has The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake up and running

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake now runs surprisingly well on phones after just a week of additional emulator development.

Legend of Zelda fans all over the world have been marveling at the Ocarina of Time remake’s visuals and enhanced gameplay systems on the Nintendo Switch 2, but the Android emulator scene has been busy marveling over something just a little bit different. One Redditor got the latest Zelda game running on Banana Native, a free emulator that’s available right now on GitHub.

Ocarina of Time remake performance has now reached a major milestone into the 30 FPS territory with frame gen, which means the game is actually running at around 15 FPS, but then scaled and interpolated using AI frame generation to appear like 30 FPS. Banana Native isn’t a traditional emulator, as it doesn’t emulate hardware. Rather, it uses the game’s own ARM64 code to run on the phone’s CPU. The Switch 2 is powered by a mobile Nvidia chip, after all.

The user is running the Ocarina of Time remake on a Poco F7 Ultra, which sports a two-generation-old Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite (Gen 4) processor. The latest phones that are coming out, like the Redmagic 12 Pro, run a 6th-gen Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme chip, so performance could be a lot better on a newer phone. Apps like Banana Native require specific driver support for each phone to run, and as I pointed out in my Redmagic 12 Pro review, platforms like Droid Deck and Game Native don’t yet have proper drivers for the newest chips.

9to5Google’s Damien Wilde recently reviewed Droid Deck, another native-type emulator that lets you legally play Steam games you own on your phone by just signing into your Steam account. It works extremely well on lots of Android phones and helps showcase just how far Android emulation has come this year.

#10402. Is another crypto winter upon us? Why Bitcoin, XRP, and Ethereum fell more than 20% in a month

The crypto markets are down again today, with major tokens suffering significant losses over the past 30 days.

As of his writing, Bitcoin is trading below $65,000, Ethereum is nearly down to $1,800, and XRP is below 96 cents.

Those are more than 20%, 25%, and 26% drops, respectively, over the past month.

Bitcoin hit an all-time high of more than $126,000 a token in October 2025, meaning its value has roughly halved since then.

Those falls are causing some to wonder whether another crypto winter is upon us. The term describes extended bear markets across cryptocurrencies, in which digital tokens drop significantly in value and stay down. Major crypto winters previously hit in 2018–2019 and 2022–2023. 

It may be too early to tell whether this is the start of another one, but several factors have been driving cryptocurrencies lower in recent weeks. Here’s what you need to know.

Expected Federal Reserve interest rate hikes

One of the greatest factors likely weighing on cryptocurrencies is the expectation that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates in December. As Reuters reported, a majority of economists expect the Fed to hike rates next month. The hike is expected to be by 25 basis points, to a range of 4.00%- 4.25%.

Rate hikes make money more expensive to borrow. This can encourage people to save, which can dampen spending and thus help fight inflation.

But when money is more expensive to borrow, those who lend it can earn more. So, when rates are higher, investors tend to pull their money from non-interest-bearing assets, like crypto, and put it into interest-bearing assets like U.S. treasury bills.

This reallocation leads to a selloff in crypto, driving the basket of digital currencies lower.

AI stock rut

Cryptocurrencies aren’t the only assets having a tough time lately.

Big Tech stocks—especially AI-adjacent ones—are having a rough few weeks. Last week was perhaps the worst thanks to the Jensen Huang scandal that sent shares of Nvdia Corporation (Nasdaq: NVDA) down more than 12% during the last five trading days.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq is also down about 1% during the same period.

AI stocks and cryptocurrencies often tend to move in tandem. Both are highly volatile and act as speculative assets. When one falls, investors tend to get jittery and sell off the other class in an effort to prevent further losses and lock in gains.

The 2026 midterm elections

A blue tsunami swept across America in early November’s midterm elections. In some ways, that is very good for the markets, as a large political majority brings a certain amount of certainty.

Investors may or may not like that party’s policy positions—but knowing what’s coming can help them plan financially.

Unfortunately for crypto, the incoming Democratic Congress may be much less friendly to the industry.

Crypto investors fear that this new political leadership could propose stronger regulation, which may stymie the industry’s growth—or at least impose checks it otherwise wouldn’t have had if the GOP had retained control of Congress.

Crypto Fear and Greed Index falls to “Extreme Fear” level

Unsurprisingly, after a 20-plus percent selloff in major tokens over the past month, investors are fretting about crypto’s future—at least in the near term. 

And nowhere is that worry more evident than when you take a look at CoinMarketCap’s Crypto Fear and Greed Index. The index tracks investor sentiment surrounding the crypto markets. It ranges from 0 to 100.

The higher the index, the more optimistic (and potentially greedy) investors tend to be about Bitcoin and other tokens. The lower the index, the more fearful they tend to be.

Right now, the index stands at a paltry 13, placing it in the “Extreme Fear” range—its lowest range. It has not been at this level since February 2026, when Bitcoin fell from around $87,500 to around $60,000 in the first few days of the month.

Of course, despite the index’s low rating—and the many factors weighing crypto down over the past month—it’s still too early to tell whether the crypto markets are on the cusp of another prolonged downturn. But the longer the rout lasts, the more the specter of another crypto winter will weigh on investors’ minds.

#10400. Nike spent years reinventing Air. Meet the new Tuned Air (exclusive)

For half a century, Nike has been synonymous with Air. The cushioning—developed at NASA, then incorporated inside a 1978 running shoe and the Air Max 1—came to represent Nike’s commitment to cutting-edge innovation. Now, with Nike on its back foot after several years of missteps, the company is counting on a new version of Air to help pull it out of its slump.

Today, a day before it announces its financial results, Nike is unveiling Tuned Air, a high-tech evolution of Air that has been in the works for years. It’s debuting this technology in a running sneaker that will come out within a year. But Nike sees Tuned Air as a broader platform that can be incorporated into other sports and even its apparel lines.

It’s one way Nike hopes to restore its credibility as an innovator and win back runners who have drifted to rivals. Given how much ground Nike has lost in recent years, it’s unclear whether this strategy will work. But the company is optimistic.

“There’s no better innovation that speaks to our formula than Air,” says Phil McCartney, Nike’s chief innovation, design, and product officer.

McCartney has spent three decades at Nike, where he ran the footwear business from 2016 until last year, when CEO Elliott Hill put him in charge of innovation, design and product across Nike, Jordan, and Converse. Speaking to me from the LeBron James Innovation Center at Nike’s campus in Beaverton, Oregon, McCartney explained that his team has a motto borrowed from two Nike legends: “Create epic shit. Make athletes better.” (The first comes from Kobe Bryant, the second from Nike’s cofounder, Bill Bowerman.)

McCartney says Nike is translating that slogan into a formula, “athlete, science, solution,” that will guide the company’s approach to innovation. His teams gather insights from athletes, then tests ideas at the Nike Sports Research Lab in Beaverton and through field teams in Eldoret, Kenya; London, and Shanghai.

Introducing Nike Tuned Air

The original Air technology created tough pockets of nitrogen using two sheets of plastic. In that case, the air was evenly distributed, creating cushioning throughout the pocket. With Tuned Air, Nike adds nuance. Before the plastic sheets are pressed together, Nike adds a chemical that allows it to create a pattern; it can now fine-tune where the gas is located and how much air is in each pocket. In doing so, it can make one part of the cushion soft and springy, and another part firm and stable. “It allows us to completely change the relationship between cushioning and support, and precision-tune the experience,” says McCartney.

Nike has given this technology to runners over the last few years. “The feedback that we’ve had from the runners who have been trying this for a couple of years now is it feels like no other cushioning system out there,” he says. “Incredibly well cushioned, but also has stability. That’s the sort of holy grail that we’ve been trying to unlock in Air.”

While Nike’s approach to achieving this balance might be distinct, many other running brands are also trying to balance cushioning with structure with their own innovations. Brooks’s DNA Tuned foam uses a dual-cell construction, with large cells in the heel to cushion landings and smaller cells in the front to make the toes more responsive. Hoka’s H-Frame features a firm strip of foam in the midsole, surrounded by softer cushioning. On’s CloudTec technology uses hollow tubes of foam molded to the bottom of the sole to absorb impact, along with a steel plate in the midsole.

With this newfound ability to modulate how much air is in each pocket, Nike can now explore “wildly different expressions” of the technology, McCartney says. Besides running, Tuned Air will be incorporated into other sports, like soccer, and into clothing like the Air Milano jacket, creating air pockets that improve temperature regulation.

Nike can even integrate Tuned Air into lifestyle shoes, like vintage sneakers, creating more comfort. “How could we make an Air Force 1 using a sock liner that is Tuned Air, so you get comfort and support?” McCartney says.

Nike has streamlined the manufacturing of Tuned Air so that it can move 70% faster than it typically does from idea to product. This is crucial to allowing Nike to be nimble as it seeks to compete with the many rivals that are also spinning out innovative new products quickly.

Nike Needs a Win

Nike needs this innovation to resonate with consumers. Last quarter, revenue declined 4% to $11.2 billion, and the company expects full-year sales to fall by a high single digit percentage. Sportswear, which accounts for nearly half the business, fell by double digits. Sales in China dropped 26% and Converse sank 28%. Nike has announced a restructuring plan that will cut more jobs after several rounds of layoffs in recent years.

Nike’s rivals have been closely observing its missteps, and taken advantage of the opportunity to steal market share. In running, a category Nike once dominated, it’s now in third place, trailing Brooks and Hoka. In the lifestyle sphere, Adidas has had hit after hit by bringing back its classic Samba and Gazelle, and New Balance has turned its retro styles like the 550 into bestsellers. Meanwhile, Nike hasn’t had a lifestyle sneaker hit in years.

Nike’s running business is starting to recover. It’s grown by double digits for more than a year, helped by the successful Vomero line. “We’re seeing market share gains almost daily right now,” says McCartney.

Historically, Nike has built running technology for elite athletes that tries to shave seconds off on their race times. But that technology takes a long time to trickle down into running shoes that the average person can lace up.

Nike doesn’t have the luxury of time anymore. That’s why its Tuned Air is designed for the everyday runner. “The entry point will be that everyday run,” McCartney says. “When you’re just trying to log your Tuesday morning run, you want the maximum amount of running with precision-tuned support.”

Nike is making a big bet on Tuned Air. But whether enough consumers get excited about the technology—and the forthcoming sneakers—to boost Nike’s fortunes is unclear. Tomorrow, when Nike lays out its long-term financial plans, we’ll get a better glimpse into how much ground it has yet to make up.

#10399. Google Pixel Tag Initial Review: The gold standard for Find Hub trackers, whatever that’s worth

Google’s Find Hub had a tumultuous launch for its performance, but also for a lack of clear direction in hardware. Over two years later, that’s finally arriving in the Google Pixel Tag which, even just a few days in, is the obvious gold standard in the race to build an AirTag for Android devices.

Google Pixel Tag is now available for purchase at the Google Store and Amazon.

There are plenty of really good Android Find Hub trackers on the market. Pebblebee and Chipolo have been long-standing examples of how to build good dual-network trackers that work on both Android and iOS, while Motorola’s Moto Tag series has delivered two Android-only trackers that deliver better performance and more focused features. But even with the Moto Tag, there’s a clear compromise. Features like the ability to ring your phone are tied to a separate app and, in turn, have some inherent clunkiness.

Pixel Tag is the device that finally brings it all together, and it’s brilliant so far.

I’ve only had the Pixel Tag for a week and, frankly, it’s impossible to properly review a tracker in that time. There are only so many ways to artificially test out how a tracker works, as most cases where you’ll find value in this sort of product can only occur in real life.

So, with that said, let’s focus on the fundamentals.

Google Pixel Tag pairs to your Android phone just like any other Find Hub tracker – though much faster compared to some others I’ve tested – but the differences are obvious towards the end of that process. The final screen shows options for setting ringer volume and an option to set up “Ring this phone.”

Those new features are what make the Pixel Tag so good, and so appealing compared to all of the competition. A quick double-tap on the Tag’s button rings whichever phone you connected it to, assuming it’s in range, and it works pretty reliably. You can also set up “left behind” alerts (now available on other Find Hub trackers too) for when the phone leaves the tracker behind – you can set up exclusion zones such as your home or work address.

One of my favorite examples of the added polish from Google is the ability to adjust the ringer volume on the page where you actually want to ring the tracker. In a crowded but quiet space where you know the tracker is close by, being able to quickly set the volume to low is a great addition. In my book, it’s the reason to buy Pixel Tag over any other Android tracker.

UWB, of course, only makes up-close finding all the better. I found this decently reliable on my Pixel 11 Pro XL, but it is a little bit frustrating that the directional cues vanish within about 10-12 feet. Fine for a backpack or something like that, potentially a problem if your Tag is attached to a set of keys.

On that note, my biggest hardware complaint is that Google took the Apple route of having no built-in mounting mechanism. The super thin and light hardware of Pixel Tag is wonderful, don’t get me wrong, but being forced to buy a separate accessory just to attach it to my bag is frustrating! One of Google’s partners, Bellroy, built one of these accessories and it’s simple enough – a silicone case with a rope. I wish I didn’t need it, but it works, and at least you get two of them in a pack for $25.

The hardware itself is pretty good across the board, really, with the battery door also being slightly easier to open compared to the Moto Tag. Inside is a standard CR2032 battery that Google says will last “over one year.” I’d personally still prefer a rechargeable battery with USB-C or wireless charging, but this is a good enough solution given the amount of time the battery lasts – hopefully Google’s claim lives up.

Rounding out some of the key aspects here, it’s worth saying that the built-in speaker is more than loud enough at its highest setting, but the value for me so far has really come in that the low setting is actually low enough to not be a nuisance. I do find it a little strange that there’s no visual indication of where the Tag’s button is, but the packaging and app both do a good enough job of letting you know.

I really just wish it would have a rechargeable battery, preferably via USB-C. It would have been the only tracker on the market to support UWB and be rechargeable.

I’m looking forward to seeing how Pixel Tag performs as the travel season spins back up, so stay tuned for a later long-term review of Google’s tracker in the coming months. Initial impressions, though, are solid. Sound off in the comments below if you have any questions around Pixel Tag, I’ll answer everything I can!

Google Pixel Tag is now available at the Google Store and Amazon.

#10398. Santa with a cause: Amazon Prime teams up with Arnold Schwarzenegger for its latest holiday campaign

After more than five decades in Hollywood, Arnold Schwarzenegger finally feels fit to play his most iconic role yet. And he’s taking the reins just in time for the holiday season.

The Terminator and Total Recall actor is suiting up in bright red and white for Amazon Prime’s new holiday creative campaign, “Santa Schwarzenegger,” which debuts on Monday.

The advertising spot begins with Schwarzenegger looking a little forlorn as the paparazzi chase him around New York. He then orders a Santa suit from Prime, allowing for anonymity as Schwarzenegger donates snacks to a dog rescue center, watches a basketball game, and heaves a Christmas tree onto the roof of a car.

“I’m at that age now and it’s believeable”

Throughout his career, Schwarzenegger has played plenty of iconic roles. He’s portrayed a killing machine from the future, Batman’s nemesis Mr. Freeze, both Hercules and his father, Zeus, and an undercover cop teaching kindergarteners.

But Schwarzenegger says no role he has ever played has been as worldwide as this one.

“This is the perfect time for me to play Santa, because I’m at that age now and it’s more believable,” Schwarzenegger tells Fast Company. “With all the interesting characters that I played in my career—from Conan to Terminator—I thought that Santa is the ultimate.”

For Amazon, the Schwarzenegger spot fits neatly into two goals: driving sales and attention to Prime, a core pillar of the online retail giant’s Black Friday, Cyber Monday, and other holiday sales events throughout the season.

But it also ties in neatly with Amazon Prime’s The Man with the Bag, an upcoming holiday film that debuts on December 2, starring Schwarzenegger as Santa for a second time.

Alan Ritchson, Awkwafina, and Ken Jeong are also featured in the film’s cast. The film also ties into Amazon’s 2026 holiday campaign, which is called “Joy Delivered.”

“Arnold is the king of the kids, we saw that when he made Kindergarten Cop,” Jo Shoesmith, Amazon’s vice president and global chief brand officer, tells Fast Company. “There is a warmth and charm to him that lives outside of the character of Santa.”

Santa “has to be in shape”

“Santa Schwarzenegger” will run through December 23 across several channels including television, digital, social, and streaming audio. Yet another component of the campaign that Amazon is promoting is Schwarzenegger’s curated holiday gift guide, which includes plush dog toys, supplements, toys intended for children and grandchildren, and dumbbells.

“Think about it, Santa has to fly all the way from the North Pole, he has to be in shape to hand out the gifts at every single continent to go to every single house,” says Schwarzenegger. “It is a lot of work. He has to be in shape.” 

There are also two books: Better Every Day, a self-help book penned by Schwarzenegger that’s due to be published in January, and Arnold, which is written about him.

There’s also a cigar lighter, which may seem counterintuitive for the fitness enthusiast, but apparently he’s smoked them for over 40 years, including during his interview with Fast Company.

“We never want to twist the arm of the personality to put something in their mouth that doesn’t come across as authentic,” says Shoesmith. “It’s very driven by his holiday ordering list.” 

As an Austrian, Schwarzenegger says his holiday traditions differed from how he raised his children in America. The holiday is celebrated on December 24 and the gift giver is a baby Jesus called Christkind, not Santa, though Schwarzenegger says the latter has become more popular there in recent years. 

“I always question with every script I get: is this something that would just be good for America, or just good for Europe, or is this something that can play in every continent,” says Schwarzenegger.

Santa, he says, is a role that can “entertain the whole world.”

The rise of star-powered Santas

While Santa has been “the face” of the Christmas holiday for marketers for more than a century, the celebrity angle has been a more recent development.

John Travolta has played the role in multiple ad spots for Capital One, while Jon Hamm did so for Fox Sports, Steve Carell for Comcast, and Brent Bailey for Target.

“He’s kind of just this joyous, universally loved figure,” adds Shoesmith. To be clear, Shoesmith was talking about Schwarzenegger at this moment, not Santa, though she says both have cross-generational appeal.

Schwarzenegger is also a safe casting choice for the retailer at a time when the American consumer isn’t optimistic. Unease about the economy was a central theme in the recent midterm elections, and the sales projection forecasts for the upcoming holiday season look fairly mixed.

Research firm Circana says average holiday spending will total $779 this year, down from $796 in 2025. The trade association the National Retail Federation is more bullish, expecting retail sales in November and December to increase 4.2% to about $1 trillion, compared to a year ago.

“We’re a brand whose logo is a smile, so joy is inherently part of who we are as a brand,” says Shoesmith of the tone approach for Amazon Prime’s campaign. “We really make sure that we have a great selection of brands at a really great price, and that’s really important for customers right now . . . they’re very price conscious.”

#10396. What is the FAA’s SMART AI system? Officials are denying a link to the nationwide ground stop

The airline ground stop that wreaked havoc on travel since Friday was not related to the FAA’s new, $875 million AI-powered system the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky, according to government officials and the artificial intelligence company behind the technology.

But the timing of the ground stop, so close to the national rollout of the Federal Aviation Administration’s SMART system, has raised questions about what the system does, its benefits and risks compared with the existing human system and what guardrails there are to address potential problems.

Officials say no connection to ground stop

The SMART system is based in a single location near Washington where a team of experts analyzes flight schedules, weather forecasts and hundreds of other streams of data. Then that office sends recommendations to the FAA’s command center, which relays them to air traffic controllers across the country for consideration.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Friday there’s no indication the communications issues that caused the ground stop are linked to the new computer system, and the top officials at the Transportation Department and FAA reiterated that Saturday.

The startup that designed the system, Air Space Intelligence, or ASI, said the ground stop wasn’t caused by “the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC.”

But lawmakers and outside groups raised questions about the SMART system before Friday’s ground stop. Last month, House Democrats sent a letter to the U.S. Government Accountability Office requesting an audit of the new software, raising concerns about safety and guardrails.

“Concerningly, the nation’s front line aviation safety workforce apparently had little to no input into SMART’s development and have received limited training and information during the current deployment process,” the Oct. 13 letter said. “The use of artificial intelligence within SMART has rightfully raised serious questions about its reliability and safety benefits, particularly on its potential to interfere with decision-making by experienced air traffic controllers or to hallucinate safety-critical information.”

SMART, however, is not — at least not yet — set up for AI to be in charge of flight control. Rather, it is making recommendations to humans who do so.

What is the SMART system?

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford unveiled the system in September, calling it a “cutting-edge tool that centralizes 200 data streams — including weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow, and controller staffing metrics — into one platform.” SMART stands for Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories.

The system’s AI-supported engine synthesizes the data systems and shows a “comprehensive visualization” of where planes are going, how much traffic the system can handle and where congestion or weather could cause problems, according to the announcement. The idea is for specialists to then use the platform to fix problems before they arise.

The FAA says that during the initial test of the system in the Washington area this fall, the system helped reroute 180 flights and saved an average of 10 minutes and 80 gallons of fuel per flight by diverting around weather or other issues. The agency said that one flight cut 42 minutes off its trip from Tampa, Florida, to Dallas thanks to the system’s recommendations.

So SMART was expanded for use nationwide on Nov. 10 for the airspace of all 22 air traffic control centers. That was three days before the ground stop.

According to a government fact sheet on the tool, SMART can predict where air traffic is headed and identify other routes before an area becomes too congested. The system can also help reopen restricted airspace faster and better manage airport arrivals.

SMART is also supposed to help with weather-related issues faster.

Currently, the FAA blocks off portions of airspace affected by weather as “large, rectangular boxes,” according to the fact sheet, which doesn’t reflect how weather actually looks, with quick-moving thunderstorms and storm systems that are “often irregular in shape, with narrow gaps or corridors that aircraft could safely fly through.”

To help with this, SMART gives the FAA and airspace operators a “clearer picture of how weather will affect air traffic over time,” allowing air traffic controllers to plan around storms and use available airspace instead of unnecessarily shutting down large areas.

No other country has a working AI air traffic tool like the SMART system, according to Michael McCormick, a former FAA airspace manager and an associate professor at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University. Eurocontrol, the European air traffic authority, has a system in testing and several manufacturers are prototyping similar tools.

Concerns around relying on AI

While government officials and ASI, the company behind SMART, have stressed that its AI system is designed to assist humans and not run flight control, its deployment has raised concerns about relying on artificial intelligence when human lives are at stake, given that even the most advanced models are prone to hallucinations — when models fabricate false information and present it as fact.

Mike O’Donnell, a former top FAA official who worked for the agency for 17 years and now does aviation safety consulting work, said the agency “has got to make sure that this is just a tool in the toolbox and not the actual machine that’s doing the work.”

The FAA, he said, “cannot afford to be wrong on this.”

“It’s good to use it with the proper guardrails and backstops to ensure that they’re not giving wrong information to controllers based on what (AI) has come up with,” O’Donnell said. “There’s got to be a way to verify and validate what it’s doing to make sure that it’s not the wrong information.”

He cautioned against putting too much trust in AI “until we know for sure that it’s proven itself time and time again. And that’s going to take a while.”

The AI system’s launch comes amid a longstanding shortage of air traffic controllers around the country. The National Air Traffic Controllers Association has been raising concerns about this for more than a decade, telling Congress in 2015 that the shortage was at a crisis level. It said then that the FAA had missed its hiring targets for five years in a row. The union represents about 14,000 controllers, roughly 3,000 of them trainees. That said, experts say no AI system can replace the human air traffic controllers who spend years training for this highly demanding and stressful job.

In an October interview with NPR, ASI co-founder and CEO Phillip Buckendorf said the SMART tool is designed for traffic managers who manage the entire U.S. airspace.

“The AI does the math, the AI does the computation,” Buckendorf told NPR, but it’s ultimately up to the human operator whether to take the system’s recommendation. “They make the decision, they are the decider, they are the judge.”

—Barbara Ortutay and Josh Funk, Associated Press

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI video generators can now turn a prompt or a character image into a few seconds of animation, and anime is one of the most popular styles people ask for. But anime is also one of the hardest styles to get right: flat colors, thin linework and stylized motion expose the weaknesses of video models quickly. For developers and designers, the useful question is not which tool is “best”, but what each one actually offers, what it cannot do yet, and how to fit it into a real production workflow.

This article compares five generators on what their own pages state, covers the problems they all share, asks whether AI anime videos are worth making, and then explains how the models work and how designers and developers can build a practical workflow, including ffmpeg and API-integration examples. “Best” here depends on the job: the tools are listed in no ranking order, each is linked once to its official site for reference, and the comparison is based on public vendor pages reviewed in November 2026. Features, models and pricing change often, so verify current details before relying on any of them.

We reviewed each vendor’s own site and compared what it states on the same points. This is a documentation-based comparison, not a lab benchmark. Where a page does not state something, we say so instead of guessing.

AI anime video generator by Pollo AI sits within a general AI video platform. On its main site, Pollo describes generating video from text prompts or uploaded images and editing existing videos, such as adding, changing, removing or restyling content. It also offers AI image generation, so a character image and the animation can be made in one place.

Strengths for anime work: text-to-video and image-to-video in the same tool, plus video editing and restyling, which suits experimenting with looks.

Limitations and gaps: the pages we could read do not name the underlying models, list credit amounts or pricing, or describe anime-specific controls such as reference characters or first and last frame inputs. You will need to test consistency yourself.

Fits: creators who want image, video and editing tools in one platform and are comfortable testing results before committing.

Vidu lists text-to-video, image-to-video and reference-to-video modes. For image-to-video you can set first and last frames. Reference-to-video lets you upload several images of a character, object or scene, and saved references can be reused through a My References feature. The site highlights 2D animation and diverse artistic styles, mentions 1080p output and offers an API platform aimed at enterprise use.

Strengths for anime work: the clearest set of consistency tools among the five pages we reviewed, with first and last frames, multi-image references and reusable saved characters.

Limitations and gaps: the page does not specify clip durations beyond examples, detail its anime-specific templates, or list prices. Free credits are mentioned without an amount.

Fits: sequences built around a recurring character, and teams that want an API.

Kling AI presents Kling 4.0 for video, described as offering stable dynamic motion and an audio-visual experience, alongside an image model, a Motion Control tool and a node-based Canvas editor for working through scripts, storyboards, images and video. It also lists MCP and CLI support for batch generation and automated production, and an API platform with documentation.

Strengths for anime work: motion-focused tooling and a workflow environment for storyboards and multi-step production, plus automation options for developers.

Limitations and gaps: the page we reviewed does not detail image-to-video specifics, first and last frame controls, camera control, durations, video resolution or pricing, and it gives no anime-specific guidance.

Fits: teams that value motion control and scripted or batch pipelines.

Hailuo AI, from MiniMax, describes creating AI videos and images from text or photos. Its page shows a reference field and an Omni Reference option, a banner for a model that mentions multimodal generation and editing, and many photo-based templates such as photo-to-motion, transformation and style transfer.

Strengths for anime work: an accessible, template-driven way to animate a still image and try stylized effects quickly.

Limitations and gaps: the page does not explain how reference works, or state camera control, durations, resolution, API availability or pricing. Template-driven results may be harder to control precisely than prompt- and frame-driven workflows.

Fits: quick experiments and social clips made from a single image.

Dreamina describes itself as an all-in-one creative platform for images, videos and talking avatars. For video it lists text-to-video, image-to-video, sketch-to-video, cartoon video generation and reference-to-video, using several Seedance models, along with editing examples such as green-screen replacement. It also offers image generation and upscaling.

Strengths for anime work: a broad toolset, including cartoon-oriented generation, references and editing in one environment.

Limitations and gaps: no official maximum duration or video resolution is stated, and the page notes that displayed pricing is for reference only and that final pricing requires signing in. The breadth of features and models can make it harder to know which one to use for a given shot.

Fits: creators who want images, video and avatars under one roof.

“Not stated” means the vendor page we reviewed did not say, not that the feature does not exist. Treat the table as a checklist of questions to answer in your own tests.

It depends on the job and on what you compare them with. Against a full studio production they are limited. Against having no animation at all, they change what a small team or solo creator can attempt.

Treat the generator as a fast prototyping and shot-making assistant, not a replacement for writing, direction and design. Audience reaction also varies, and some viewers are openly critical of AI-made work, so quality and disclosure both matter.

Most current generators are diffusion models extended to video. As in image diffusion, the model starts from random noise and removes it step by step, guided by your inputs. The extension to video, described in research such as Video Diffusion Models, is that the model denoises a whole sequence of frames together, so that motion and appearance stay coherent over time. Many systems work in a compressed latent space rather than on raw pixels to keep generation affordable.

Create an original character sheet with front, side and three-quarter views, a fixed color palette and a clear silhouette. Keep it simple: fewer fine details means less flicker.

Break the sequence into short shots with one action and one camera move each. A four-shot, twenty-second sequence is more realistic than one long generation.

Start each shot from a clean keyframe of your character. Where a tool supports first and last frames or reference images, use them to define the pose and keep identity stable.

Describe subject, action, camera and mood, and add a style anchor. For example: “The girl slowly turns toward the camera, wind moves her hair, petals drift past, gentle push-in, 2D cel shading, clean linework.”

Scrub through each clip for warped hands, drifting faces and flickering lines. Discard or regenerate failures instead of hoping nobody notices.

Join the best takes, color-match them, add sound and captions, and add disclosure where a platform requires it.

Developers can make the pipeline repeatable. Two patterns help: scripted post-processing with ffmpeg, and a resilient job-based client for any generation API.

The script below extracts a last frame to seed the next shot, normalizes clips to a common size and frame rate so they can be joined, concatenates them, and optionally holds each frame twice for an “on twos” look. Adjust sizes and frame rates to your project.

Video generation is usually asynchronous: you submit a job, then poll or receive a callback. The sketch below shows the pattern with a timeout and backoff. The endpoints and fields are placeholders, so follow your provider’s documentation for real ones.

Most are diffusion models for video. They start from noise and remove it step by step across a sequence of frames, guided by a text prompt and often a starting image or reference images, until coherent motion appears.

Usually, for consistency. The image locks the character and style, while the prompt only needs to describe motion.

Thin lines and flat color regions make small frame-to-frame changes visible. Simpler designs, slower motion and post-processing reduce it.

Partly. Reference images, saved characters and shared keyframes help, but you should still review every shot for drift.

For short clips, concept previews and storyboards, often yes. For long, dialogue-driven stories, not yet.

It depends on the tool and plan. Read the current terms and make sure you have rights to any characters or assets you upload.

Run the same character image and prompt through each, then compare consistency, line stability, motion quality and cost per usable second.

AI anime video generators are useful, but uneven. The five tools reviewed here differ in input modes, consistency tools, developer access and how much their own pages say, and none removes the core problems of consistency, flicker and limited acting. The practical approach is to test several tools on the same shots, keep your workflow tool-agnostic, design characters that are simple and consistent, and review every clip before it ships. Used that way, they are a capable prototyping and shot-making aid, not a substitute for design and direction.

#10392. Google Fi brings back network switching with ‘secondary’ partner, expands W+ beyond Pixel

Google Fi Wireless is rolling out a big update today with the return of network switching thanks to a “secondary” partner.

Google Fi is now bringing back a second partner as part of its new “super network.” Most users will be on the “Primary network,” but Google Fi will automatically switch users to the “Secondary network” if it meaningfully improves performance with so-called “smart thresholds” for doing so. At launch, there is no manual switching.

Google is not naming the second network today, but did share that Ultra Wideband is supported. Officially, you are switching between “two of America’s fastest 5G networks.”

Network switching will first be supported on Pixel 9 and newer devices that have a Google Fi eSIM (and no other SIM active). It makes use of Android’s Multiple Enabled Profiles (MEP) eSIM technology that allows for two carrier profiles on a single chip.

It might be important to note that T-Mobile actually bought out Sprint, and added their towers to their network so its safe to say that Google Fi still works with the same coverage as before the merger.

The Google Fi app gains a “Your super network” card in the Home tab that shows whether you’re connected to the Primary or Secondary network. “See activity” lets you view switching history and when it last occurred. Google will also note if you’re in range of W+ networks.

Google today is also expanding its Wi-Fi Auto Connect+ network beyond Pixel phones to select Samsung Galaxy (S23, Fold/Flip 5, and newer) and modern Motorola phones. These premium Wi-Fi networks are available in millions of airports, malls, stores, and restaurants. The connection happens automatically, with the Google Fi Virtual Carrier Network encrypting data.

The final update today sees the companion app gain “Ask Fi.” This AI-powered chat is meant to quickly provide answers and guided troubleshooting for common issues. You can request human support with seamless handoff that keeps the chat context.

These Google Fi updates start rolling out today, with network switching seeing gradual availability. This launch is accompanied by several deals:

Can you be Nvidia's next CEO, old friend?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nvidia's board of directors has approached Arm chief executive Rene Haas as a potential successor to Jensen Huang, according to a report from the Financial Times that cites people familiar with the matter. Haas is among several candidates under consideration, although it remains unclear whether he will get a formal offer and/or agree to take the position.

The search for Nvidia's next chief executive comes as the company undergoes a leadership transition following Jensen Huang's swift departure from the CEO position earlier this week. For now, Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress serves as interim CEO. The company's board is currently searching for a permanent replacement and is reportedly evaluating both internal and external candidates. Neither Arm nor Nvidia commented on the matter to FT.

Rene Haas is no stranger to Nvidia, as he spent approximately seven years at the company before leaving in 2013. During his tenure as vice president at Nvidia, he was responsible for multiple projects, including notebook GPUs, Windows-on-Arm, and Tegra system-on-chips. Given that he held senior management positions, he certainly gained experience with Nvidia's operations, corporate culture, and relationships with customers and partners.

Furthermore, Haas has experience with the development of consumer and data center CPUs as well as GPUs and GPU IP, a combination that is hard to find in the industry. Haas reportedly maintains close ties with Jensen Huang and several members of Nvidia's board, which could make him a particularly attractive candidate for a company whose strategy and management structure have orbited around its founder for more than three decades.

While at Arm, Haas has demonstrated a willingness to make substantial strategic changes at the company. Since Haas took the reins in 2022, Arm has introduced its Compute Subsystems (CSS) initiative, providing customers with complete and validated processor platform design, making it easier for newcomers to enter the market. Arm also introduced its first own-brand AGI CPU, putting the company in direct competition with some of its traditional customers. Both initiatives represent significant departures from Arm's traditional business model; however, they demonstrate Haas' readiness to pursue new revenue opportunities despite risks and the possibility of damaging relationships with long-term partners.

Another advantage is Haas' extensive experience with the semiconductor industry in general. Arm's CPU and GPU technologies are used in system-on-chips developed by hundreds of companies that have very distinctive requirements, including Nvidia itself, Apple, Qualcomm, and MediaTek, just to name a few.

In addition, Haas led Arm through its initial public offering in 2023 and therefore has experience with investors and regulators. Also, Haas happens to be the CEO of SoftBank, the parent of Arm.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Nevertheless, Haas' potential appointment would not be without challenges, primarily because he has never managed a company the scale of Nvidia. Arm has around 10,000 employees worldwide; it develops and licenses various semiconductor IP, primarily CPU and GPU technologies, to a wide range of customers with distinct needs. By contrast, Nvidia designs CPUs, GPUs, networking equipment, complete AI systems, and software platforms and has a headcount of about 42,000. As a result, if Haas becomes the boss of Nvidia, he will have to manage a considerably bigger organization with a dramatically more complicated product portfolio and supply chain. Furthermore, replacing Huang, who has led Nvidia since its establishment in 1993 and personally shaped its technology strategy and business tactics, would be a formidable task for virtually any executive.

Ironically, Haas' appointment (if it happens) would create an unusual situation in which Nvidia will be led by the chief executive of a company it attempted to acquire in 2020 and abandoned the transaction in 2022 amid regulatory opposition.

#10388. Three Questions (And Answers) To Secure The AI-Enabled Workplace

Pieter Danhieux is the Co-Founder and Chairman/CEO of Secure Code Warrior.

​If any workplace maxim has proven true in the 21st century, it’s that every employee is a technologist.​

Today’s professionals are, after all, universally reliant on devices, software, the internet and cloud services to manage timesheets, research marketing reports, submit budgets, diagnose operational issues and pursue innovation. The fact that all of this has grown so commonplace illustrates how technology is increasingly demystified and democratized. Once considered fairly esoteric—unknowable, save for those on IT teams—these advancements are now easy to instantly obtain and consume for those in any department.​

So, it should come as no surprise that these professionals are deploying AI just like any other technology: Most senior business and technology leaders say AI is embedded into core functions and “deployed broadly” across the enterprise. Four of five expect AI agents to make key, impactful decisions for their organization within the next year. Three of five say their company has redesigned job roles to prepare specifically for an AI-enabled workplace.​

But there remains a critical—and relatively unaddressed—issue: AI adoption is expanding faster than AI readiness. Less than one-quarter of those senior business and technology leaders believe their staffers are fully ready for AI. Nearly four of five agree that the speed of AI will outpace their organization’s governance models.

For certain, employees will always be capable of harnessing AI to boost productivity. But they often do so without an understanding of the security implications of connecting tools, granting permissions, sharing information or allowing an AI agent to act on their behalf.​ In response, security leaders need to find out who’s using AI agents, what data and access employees are allowing for them, what the agents are empowered to do and whether teams are able to recognize when an AI-powered workflow emerges as unsafe.​

To arrive at this level of heightened awareness, these leaders must address the following three questions:​

​This is a complex line of pursuit because adoption is so decentralized, with “shadow AI” highly pervasive. According to results from a 2026 PagerDuty survey, two-thirds of office professionals say they’ve used AI tools or services on the job, even though they realized the activity wasn’t permitted by their company’s policies.

​As a result, shadow AI becomes an organizational problem. Employees can move from chatting with an AI assistant to building workflows and automations without ever thinking of themselves as AI developers. Banning these tools rarely works because employees adopt them for a simple reason: They make work easier.

Instead, security and business leaders should pair visibility and governance with AI literacy, so employees have the skills to make safe decisions themselves. Part of that literacy is understanding that LLMs and other AI assistants can’t be trusted to produce secure code on their own. Without training in what to look for and how these tools go wrong, even simple automations and coding projects can introduce unacceptable risk.

​Most employees would never deliberately share confidential company information with an unknown third party. Yet, many don’t think twice about doing so with an AI assistant.

​In fact, according to the same PagerDuty survey, “88% of office professionals have shared work-related information with public AI tools such as ChatGPT.” Additionally, “43% have shared emails or other correspondence, 40% have shared meeting notes or summaries, 34% have input customer data or information and 31% have shared financial information or confidential company documents and strategies.”​

​Acceptable-use policies are necessary, but they can’t fix this on their own. The goal is behavior change, not just awareness. Employees need practical judgment and responsible habits that shape what they actually do with AI, not just what they know about it. Before connections are made, staffers should ask, “Does AI really need this access? What can it do with the permissions I’m granting? What could happen if it behaves unexpectedly?” In the process, they’ll gain an understanding of and appreciation for zero-trust principles that enforce least privilege.​

​Ultimately, it’s about accountability. Policies are meaningless without workforce buy-in.

​Governance should go beyond “rules” and technical controls to ensure teams possess the skills and mindsets required to use AI responsibly whenever they share data, connect a system, grant access or automate an action. But compliance shouldn’t become the end goal. The more important goal is to ensure training changes what an employee does at the moment they share data, connect a system, grant access or automate an action—for example, if they immediately detect an unsafe automation or permission before it emerges as a security incident.

​Your employees are already using AI. The only question is whether they’ve been trained to use it well. Ultimately, employees must understand that giving an AI agent access is a risk decision, even if it doesn’t seem like one.

​Toward this goal, security leaders should pair technical governance with workforce capabilities, with insights about adoption, guardrails and practical education that enable employees to pursue all of the advantages of AI innovation while still operating safely.

​Restrictions alone can’t do this—not when everybody is a technologist who can get around the rules if they feel it’s necessary. However, when these same employees not only know the guardrails but why they matter, they benefit their organizations by leveraging AI advancements without unduly increasing risk.​

Better late than never for ATI's first unified shader cards.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A newly accepted kernel patch slated for the upcoming Linux 7.5 release finally resolves a long-standing hardware video decoding bug on AMD's ancient R600 architecture, nearly two decades after the cards first hit store shelves. As spotted by Phoronix, the fix targets the Unified Video Decoder (UVD) engine across the RV610, RV620, RV630, RV635, and RV670 silicon families, making up the Radeon HD 2000 and HD 3000 families released starting in 2007. Linux users running these cards experienced visual corruption during hardware-accelerated video playback whenever the GPU was simultaneously handling active 3D or desktop drawing workloads; those issues should now be resolved.

I investigated video corruption on my older iMac7,1 (RV610/M74, device ID 1002:94c8). When the decoder was reading compressed video from system memory while the GPU was drawing, it would corrupt video frames. Moving the input to VRAM allowed frames to decode correctly. Disabling graphics draws also stopped the corruption. Here is a proposal to keep UVD buffers in VRAM for this family of devices, as the driver already does for some other chips. The patch covers RV610, RV620, RV630, RV635 and RV670. These chips share the RV6xx decoder path and legacy R600 firmware, so I think they are likely to have the same hardware requirements. Someone with the other hardware would need to verify that. I tested this on Debian. I used Codex to help with the investigation, testing and patch.

Interestingly, the breakthrough didn't come from a grizzled veteran of the open-source graphics stack, but from a newcomer utilizing OpenAI's Codex to help untangle the legacy driver path. The culprit turned out to be a memory placement oversight: the driver wasn't consistently keeping UVD input buffers pinned inside dedicated VRAM. When graphics draw calls competed for resources, frames failed to decode properly. By forcing those buffers to stay in VRAM — a behavior the Radeon kernel driver apparently already enforced for several other chip families — video playback cleans right up.

It is easy to forget just how pivotal the R600 generation was for PC graphics. Launching in 2007 as the first desktop GPU lineup built under the AMD banner following that firm's blockbuster acquisition of the Canadian ATI Technologies Inc., the Radeon HD 2000 series marked the new AMD graphics division's transition away from separate pixel and vertex pipelines on the desktop, after implementing the tech first for the Xbox 360. The move to a unified shader architecture arrived alongside DirectX 10 and Windows Vista, so it was a time of many transitions.

While the flagship Radeon HD 2900 XT famously struggled against Nvidia's dominant GeForce 8800 GTX in raw gaming rasterization and power draw, the R600 family brought serious multimedia chops to the table. The introduction of the first-generation Unified Video Decoder (UVD) on the mainstream RV610 and RV630 chips, and later the refined RV670 powering the beloved Radeon HD 3850 and 3870, allowed even budget PCs to offload heavy H.264 and VC-1 Blu-ray decoding from the CPU. In 2007, smooth 1080p playback without maxing out a dual-core processor was a major selling point for many users, but none more so than home theater PC (HTPC) builders.

Of course, almost nobody is daily driving a TeraScale 1 graphics card in 2026, especially when modern integrated graphics run circles around them at a fraction of the wattage; the contributor who submitted the patches wants them for his ancient Core 2 Duo-based iMac. Yet, there is something quietly heartwarming about the longevity of open-source Linux drivers. Whereas proprietary Windows support for the HD 2000 and 3000 series was sunsetted over a decade ago, the mainline Linux kernel continues to carry the torch. Combined with recent AI-assisted cleanup efforts across the Mesa R600 user-space driver, vintage Radeon hardware is arguably in better software shape today than it was during its actual retail lifespan.

#10385. Wyze’s new door lock has speedy fingerprint recognition and 12-month battery life

Wyze is today launching its new “Lever Lock,” a smart lock for your front door that has a year of battery life and fast fingerprint recognition, all for an affordable price tag.

Available starting today, the Wyze Level Lock is not your typical deadbolt smart lock. Rather, this is a smart lock designed for your standard single-bore latch, meaning it’s available for doors that other smart locks aren’t compatible with. You can still have a deadbolt, but you’ll need enough space for both (per Wyze’s guidelines below).

The Lever Lock has a PIN entry and a fingerprint sensor, the latter of which Wyze says recognizes your fingerprint in about half a second. It uses local storage for biometric data and works to improve that data with each successful unlock.

The PIN has a clever feature (though it’s presented in somewhat poor taste) that lets you input random digits before or after your actual code to prevent onlookers from being able to see your code. There’s also a physical key backup as well as a USB-C input on the outside in the case that the battery dies – Wyze says it lasts about 12 months on a charge using eight AA batteries.

The Wyze Lever Lock is available today for $99.98 and shipping immediately.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Adam Turaj, a Mechatronics Engineering student at the University of Waterloo, built an open-source LEGO 3D printer named “Studprint” with only 13 pieces of the printer not made out of LEGO. The bill of materials only totals $173.35, with $30 of the budget going to LEGO pieces that comprise 92% of the whole build. Turaj’s project got him flown to the Rocky Mountain RepRap Festival 2026, where he got to meet Prusa CMO Zack Freedman and presented Studprint to over 4,000 people at the event.

Earlier this year, Hack Club posted a challenge called Infill, calling makers and hobbyists to design their own 3D printers from scratch and receive a $350 grant to build their printers. Whoever submits a benchy with their printer gets a chance to be flown to the Rocky Mountain RepRap Festival 2026, and Turaj was one of them.

Turaj joined this challenge, designing his LEGO 3D printer in SOLIDWORKS. He named the project Studprint, referring to the studs on a LEGO brick. What takes this project even farther is that Turaj decided he would only use “classical LEGO,” avoiding LEGO Technic pieces wherever possible. Looking at the repository’s images of the CAD designs, you would easily mistake it for a virtual LEGO builder.

Turaj shared an image of the bill of materials (BOM) on the GitHub repository for his build, showing a final build price of $173.35. There are three major electronics components in the printer: the first is the BTT SKR Pico V1.0, a control board commonly used in open-source 3D printers like the Voron V0; for wireless capability, a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W is used; and the whole printer is powered by a Mean Well LRS-150-24 switching power supply — with all three components priced at around $25 each. This printer is built with the backbone of a true DIY 3D-printer build, unlike this cute LEGO 3D printer we covered last year that used a 3D printing pen.

There are five NEMA 17 stepper motors, also popular in 3D printers, whether open- or closed-source. Four of the motors control the axes, while the fifth is used to feed filament to the Trianglelab V6 Extruder. The rest of the 3D printer is made of $30 worth of LEGO pieces; even the build plate is a block of LEGO. Turaj’s only print shown on the GitHub repository is a Benchy, sliced in Klipper and printed in 1.25 hours; it’s surprisingly good considering the leadscrews are all LEGO pieces.

#10382. November 2026 Pixel Drop: Create My Widget, HiLight for Google Messages, Pixel 10 Rambler, & more

Like last year, the next Pixel Drop is rolling out a month early in November. Coupled with Android 17 QPR2, it’s quite a big Feature Drop for Gemini and other AI capabilities, as well as the Pixel 10 series.

Pixel Watch Drop: Create My Widget, Phone-to-Watch Unlock, and Wear OS 7.1

Gemini Intelligence is coming to the Pixel 10, Pixel 10 Pro, Pixel 10 Pro XL, and Pixel 10 Pro Fold. The lead feature is Rambler to automatically remove filler words and format your transcription.

The Pixel 10 series also gets Gemini app automation for ordering groceries, ride-sharing, meal delivery, marketplace transactions, and booking reservations. Proactive Gemini Actions let you “send groceries right to your Google Keep list straight from ongoing conversations” and more.

The Pixel 11 and 10 are getting Create My Widget. This generative UI capability lets you create custom homescreen objects using natural language. For example, you can create a sports widget or an event countdown. The feature first debuted on Googlebooks.

On the Pixel 11, Gemini Call Screen is an “intelligent, proactive assistant that screens incoming inquiries on demand.” Replacing Manual Call Screen, Gemini will speak to callers in a more conversational manner than before.

Meanwhile, the Pixel 10+ now lets Gemini make calls on your behalf in the US. Use cases include changing reservations, putting items on hold, and checking inventory. Beta testing started in September.

The AI features continue with 10 new Custom Icon styles. Following the March introduction, Google has upgraded the experience with Nano Banana for higher-quality icons. Available on Pixel 6a+.

Pixel Solver in the Google Calculator app provides generative AI custom templates and allows for conversational, multi-step problem solving using prompts. This is available on Pixel 11+.

Unit Conversion is a “top-tier module” that saves you from switching between your browser and the Calculator app. It offers inline mathematics, combined unit interpretation, and real-time exchange rates on the Pixel 6a+.

On the Pixel 11 Pro, Pro XL, and Pro Fold, HiLight now supports Google Messages notifications after being restricted to phone calls and Gemini at launch.

Pixel Search is now available on the Pixel 6 and newer to provide a more integrated on-device lookup experience that spans apps, web, settings, and other personal content. It allows for natural language search from the search bar at the top of the app grid.

I suspect a lot of these will be server side/app updates. When I went to settings to check for the update I already noticed the new family hub so it was live even before I installed the new version.

One thing I noticed immediately on my 9 Pro is that the battery life is much better. It's been pretty abysmal lately, I thought it might battery degradation but here we are, it's much improved, fingers crossed it'll stay like that. That alone was worth the update.

Extreme Battery Charging is now available on the Pixel 10 series.

Following the 2.0 redesign in September, Pixel VIPs now supports Live Location Sharing. This will surface real-time information and battery status from Find Hub in contact cards and homescreen widgets on the Pixel 6a+.

Transit Mode has been upgraded to automatically trigger based on device sensors. This is available on the Pixel 6a+.
